title: Pressure ulcers (bedsores)
intro: Pressure ulcers are injuries to skin and underlying tissue caused by prolonged pressure, usually over bony areas such as the heels, hips, tailbone and elbows. They affect people who cannot move easily, such as those who are bedridden or in a wheelchair. They can be prevented in most cases by regular repositioning and careful skin care.

sections.heading: How they develop
paragraphs: When pressure compresses skin against bone for long, blood supply is reduced and the tissue is damaged. Friction, shearing when sliding down in bed, moisture from sweat or incontinence, poor nutrition, reduced sensation and older age increase the risk. Diabetes, circulation disease and paralysis also contribute.

sections.heading: Stages
paragraphs: The first sign is persistent redness that does not fade when pressed. Next the skin may blister or break, then deeper damage reveals fat, muscle or bone. Pain, warmth, swelling and drainage may signal infection. Early recognition prevents progression.

sections.heading: Prevention
paragraphs: Change position at least every few hours in bed or shift weight every fifteen to thirty minutes in a chair, as advised for the person. Use pressure-relieving mattresses and cushions, keep the skin clean and dry, manage incontinence, avoid dragging skin across sheets, and keep the heels free of pressure with pillows. Inspect skin daily, particularly over bony areas. Adequate protein, calories and fluids support skin health.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Relieving pressure is essential, otherwise wounds will not heal. Wounds are cleaned, kept moist with suitable dressings and dead tissue may be removed by wound specialists. Infection is treated with antibiotics when necessary. Deep ulcers may need surgery. Pain relief and nutritional support are important. Negative pressure treatment is sometimes used.

sections.heading: Support for caregivers
paragraphs: Carers should learn safe techniques for turning and moving a person. Ask nurses to demonstrate. Seek help quickly if redness persists, a wound appears or the person has fever. Care plans and aids may be arranged through nursing services.

examples.title: Setting up a turning schedule
examples.text: Imagine you care for a relative who stays in bed most of the day. You could write a repositioning schedule, use a pressure-relieving mattress and check the heels and tailbone each morning and evening.

examples.title: Spotting early signs
examples.text: Suppose you notice a red patch that stays red after pressure is removed. You might take the pressure off the area at once and contact the nurse or doctor.
